data.title: Trump says Starlink access restored. Ukraine is reporting more interruptions.
data.description:
Trump says Starlink access restored, but Ukraine reports more interruptions

Victoria Craw and Anastacia Galouchka, (c) 2026 , The Washington Post
Updated Fri, October 23, 2026 at 11:01 AM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

President Donald Trump said Elon Musk has lifted restrictions on Ukraine's access to Starshield, the military equivalent of Starlink, amid confusion over who previously ordered access to the network be curtailed.

Trump declined to comment on reports that he called the SpaceX chief executive to ask Ukraine's access to the satellite network be fully reinstated, but described his relationship with Musk as "a very good one." The "bottom line" was that Musk had "put it back," he said in comments to reporters on Thursday.

Subscribe to The Post Most newsletter for the most important and interesting stories from The Washington Post.

Advertisement

However, Ukrainian soldiers said Friday they were still experiencing Starshield disruptions, with no indication that any restrictions had been lifted.

On Friday, Starshield was still operating "with constant interruptions," although at a higher speed than on Thursday, Ukrainian commander Andriy "Klima" Klymenko, commander of the 414th Unmanned Systems Brigade, told The Washington Post.

"Right now we don't notice that restrictions on Starlink have been lifted," Serhii Beskrestnov, an adviser to Ukraine's defense ministry, wrote in a statement.

Ukraine's military access to Starshield, a secure satellite network designed for government use, was unexpectedly throttled last week, impeding Ukraine's midrange strike campaign on Russian-occupied territory. There is confusion over who ordered access to the network be curtailed, with both Musk and Trump suggesting it was the other side.

The curtailed service followed Trump's announcement of a diesel deal with Russia and demands that Ukraine halt strikes on Russian oil refineries, as he sought to address high energy prices ahead of the midterm elections.

The Trump administration has faced repeated questions over why access to Starshield was curtailed and who ordered it. The Wall Street Journal reported this week that Musk ordered the slowdown and Trump called him to ask it be lifted.

The White House and Musk did not immediately respond to an overnight request for comment.

Trump has recently increased pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky to make a deal to end Russia's war against Ukraine, called for his ouster and waived punishing sanctions against Moscow.

Earlier this week, Russia agreed to start restart trilateral talks with Ukrainian representatives, following a meeting between U.S. envoy Steve Witkoff and Russian President Vladimir Putin. On Friday, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said talks were planned for the first half of November, in Abu Dhabi.

On Thursday, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Connecticut), the senior Democrat on the Senate's permanent subcommittee on ​investigations, said he had opened an inquiry into the restrictions to Starshield services.

In a letter to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Blumenthal said it raises questions about who has the technical and legal authority to make such changes and whether the U.S. military had sufficient alternatives if SpaceX-provided services became unavailable.

Sen. Thom Tillis (R-North Carolina) said Thursday that "innocent Ukrainians have bore the murderous brunt," of limited access to the technology.

"We've spent that week trying to determine the party responsible, but they have yet to own the decision, if in fact one was made," he said. "I have full confidence in the powers of the United States Government and SpaceX to solve this, if there are indeed no objections."

Vice President JD Vance said Thursday it was "completely understandable" that Musk did not want to get involved in the war as he runs a private company.

"I don't think this is about Elon. I think it's fundamentally, what is America's policy in Ukraine and Russia going to be," Vance said.

data.title: Melania Trump secures ceasefire in Russian-held Ukrainian city, White House says
data.description:
Russia, Ukraine agree to Oleshky ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump, White House says

By Steve Holland and Ryan Patrick Jones
Fri, October 23, 2026 at 1:56 PM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

FILE PHOTO: Drone footage shows destruction in the Russian occupied city of Oleshky

1 of 2
FILE PHOTO: A still image taken from an undated drone video released September 24, 2026, shows destroyed vehicles sitting on a street in Oleshky, Kherson Region, Russian-controlled Ukraine. 34th Separate Marine Brigade "Borysfen"/Handout via REUTERS

By Steve Holland and Ryan Patrick Jones

WASHINGTON, Oct 23 (Reuters) - US first lady Melania Trump has secured a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in the Russian-controlled city ‌of Oleshky, which will begin on October 29, the White House said on Friday.

Residents of ‌the southern Ukrainian town, occupied by Russian forces since February 2022, have reported a deepening food crisis.

"Both nations agreed ​to temporarily stop all military action in Oleshky to allow for humanitarian aid to enter and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway," a White House statement said.

Advertisement

The development comes as Melania Trump's husband, President Donald Trump, pressures Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy to reach an agreement with Russian ‌President Vladimir Putin to end the ⁠war, which began when Russia invaded Ukraine in February 2022.

Melania Trump has been active in trying to get Ukrainian children seized by Russia during the ⁠war returned to their families.

"The situation in Oleshky is dire. Oleshky is a front-line war city on the brink of disaster. Oleshky's remaining population is comprised primarily of elderly residents who urgently need medical attention, ​medicine, ​food, and clean water," Melania Trump said in the ​statement.

The ceasefire will allow non-military teams from ‌both countries to visit residents in their homes and coordinate transportation for those wishing to evacuate to either Russia or Ukraine, with an unnamed American media organization accompanying the teams to document the process, the first lady said.

Newsmax, a right-leaning news outlet, said in a report that its cameras would be granted "exclusive access to document the effort."

Oleshky, located across the Dnipro River from Kherson, has ‌a remaining population of 1,700 to 2,000 people — primarily ​elderly residents, along with about 50 children — down from ​roughly 24,000 before the war, the White ​House said. About 90% of the city was flooded following the destruction of ‌the Kakhovka Dam, according to the White ​House.

The statement said Melania ​Trump and her representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to define the terms of the localized ceasefire.

"Residents who wish to evacuate will receive coordinated support and transportation to ​their preferred destination. I anticipate ‌some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine," Melania Trump said.

(Reporting ​by Steve Holland and Susan Heavey; Writing by Ryan Patrick Jones in Toronto; Editing ​by Katharine Jackson, David Ljunggren and Caitlin Webber)

data.title: Israel orders army to prepare for full closure of West Bank after alleged attack
data.description:
Israel orders closure of the West Bank after soldiers kill 2 Palestinians behind an alleged attack

SHLOMO MOR and SAM MEDNICK
Updated Fri, October 23, 2026 at 6:44 AM UTC
3 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Israel Shooting Attack

1 of 3
Israeli soldiers and emergency personnel gather near ambulances following a shooting attack near Yehuda Junction, near Hebron, in the occupied West Bank, Friday, Oct. 23, 2026. (AP Photo/Mahmoud Illean) (AP Photo/Mahmoud Illean)

HEBRON, West Bank (AP) — Israeli soldiers shot and killed two Palestinians who the military said had launched an attack near the city of Hebron in the occupied West Bank on Friday morning. At least five people were injured, including some critically.

The deadly shooting is likely to further add to political tensions and mounting security concerns ahead of Israel's key parliamentary election next week.

The army said it prevented a "terror attack against Israeli civilians" and that the gunmen carried an M16 rifle and a handgun. It said the two men were Palestinians from Hebron and that they were both killed. It did not elaborate on the target of their alleged attack. There was also no word on the identities of those injured.

Advertisement

A few hours later, Israel ordered the army to prepare for a full closure of the West Bank. The office of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said it instructed security forces to immediately cordon off the city of Hebron and prepare to fully close all of the West Bank, starting Friday.

Israeli voters will decide next Tuesday whether to grant Netanyahu yet another term as prime minister — or usher in a new era of Israeli politics. The election comes three years after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel that triggered the war in Gaza.

Israel's government has warned of potential attacks by the country's "enemies" in the lead-up to the election.

Netanyahu holds an emergency meeting

Following the shooting, Netanyahu held an emergency meeting of his Security Cabinet and officials from top military and security agencies. He blamed Hamas, saying the militant group was "planning a major attack aimed at murdering innocent civilians."

"Our brave soldiers thwarted this attack with courage and determination," he said, without elaborating on what the planned attack entailed.

"I commend them for their actions and wish our wounded a speedy recovery," he added but did not say if the wounded were soldiers or civilians.

Earlier Friday, Israel's far-right national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, known for extremist views, said that the attack shows that Israel needs to restrict the Palestinians' freedom of movement in the West Bank.

"The lives of the residents of Judea and Samaria, of the settlers, the lives of the soldiers, the lives of the police officers, the lives of our fighters are a million times more important than freedom of movement," he said, using an Israeli reference to the West Bank.

Ahead of the anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas-led attack that triggered the war, Netanyahu said the Palestinian militant group could attack Israel in a bid to influence the outcome of the elections. He did not provide evidence to back up the claim.

The injured are evacuated to a hospital, medics say

Emergency responders said five people were injured, some critically, and were being evacuated to hospitals in Israel. A statement from the responders said gunfire was still ongoing as they arrived at the scene of the attack near the Yehuda Junction in the morning.

Two men in their 20s had gunshot wounds to their lower limbs, and one was unconscious and seriously injured, the responders said.

"We arrived at a difficult scene while shooting was still taking place in the area," said Tzuriel Edri with the response team.

An investigation was underway, authorities said.

Also Friday, the army said soldiers and Israeli security and intelligence agencies conducted dozens of operations in the West Bank and apprehended dozens of people, including those affiliated with Hamas and Islamic Jihad militant groups. It also said it had located weapons, including M16 rifles and submachine guns.

Closures of the West Bank, such as the one ordered Friday, are growing more common in the territory. It's the fourth time in the past month that Israel has imposed restrictions across the area, shutting gates and checkpoints connecting Palestinian villages to major roads.

Meanwhile, Israeli roads in the territory remain open to Israeli drivers, including settlers, who can still travel through the area but may face delays.

data.title: In face of GOP backlash, Trump praises Ramaswamy ad featuring Amy Acton's mother
data.description:
Politics

Trump says he recommended "powerful" Ramaswamy ad featuring Amy Acton's estranged mother stay up

By
Kathryn Watson
Politics Reporter
Kathryn Watson is a politics reporter for CBS News Digital, based in Washington, D.C.
Read Full Bio
Kathryn Watson,
Caroline Linton
Associate Managing Editor, Politics
Caroline Linton is an associate managing editor on the political team for CBSNews.com. She has previously written for The Daily Beast, Newsweek and amNewYork.
Read Full Bio
Caroline Linton

Updated on: October 22, 2026 / 9:00 PM EDT / CBS News

Add CBS News on Google

Washington — President Trump on Thursday praised the "very powerful ad" Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy is running featuring the estranged mother of Democratic gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton, after the ad drew pushback from some Republicans like Ohio Gov. Mike DeWine.

Mr. Trump posted on Truth Social that he suggested Ramaswamy keep the ad up, saying the press is "trying to convince everyone that this Ad is bad, because it's so good!" 

The ad, which first circulated on social media on Monday and is now television, features Acton's estranged mother, Donna Arthur, who called Acton a "liar" and sought to undermine her credibility. Acton's campaign condemned the ad, and her brother, Philip Stearns, called it a "despicable low." 

According to court documents provided by the campaign, Arthur's now-deceased husband was charged with raping Acton, which she said occurred when she was between 10 and 12 years old. He entered a not guilty plea and left the area while out on bond; the case never went to trial.

DeWine on Thursday said he thought the Ramaswamy campaign should take the ad down. "It's wrong to run this ad," the Ohio Republican told reporters. "I would urge Ramaswamy's campaign to take this down." DeWine did not rescind his endorsement. 

But Vice President JD Vance and now Mr. Trump are defending the ad and using it to criticize Acton. 

"Vivek Ramaswamy put up a very powerful Ad about a mother saying that her daughter, Amy Acton, who is running for Governor of Ohio, is a liar, and much worse," Mr. Trump wrote in his social media post. "The Press, in a concerted and well coordinated attack, is trying to get Vivek Ramaswamy to 'take down the Ad.' Frankly, anybody whose mother spoke about a daughter in that way would normally lead to the daughter being precluded from serving in Office, let alone the Office of Governor."

In his post, Mr. Trump did not mention why Acton and her birth mother are estranged, or any of the family's backstory. 

Shortly after his post, on the White House South Lawn, reporters told Mr. Trump the backstory — that Acton's mother stayed married to the man charged with raping her. CBS News senior White House reporter Weijia Jiang asked the president why anyone should listen to what the estranged mother has to say. 

"Well I know nothing about it," the president responded. "All I know is the mother said very bad things about Acton, who I guess is running for governor against Vivek. And all I can say is Vivek is great. And I know one thing, if my mother said bad about me, it would be a major news story, that's for sure. So I don't know what it is, but I guess the mother said very bad things about the one who's running for governor. And I think you have to say that seriously." 

"I'm defending it because I know that if that ad were about my mother, you would love it, you would love every inch of it," Mr. Trump added. 

In his Truth Social post, the president specifically went after DeWine.

"Our RINO Governor of Ohio, Mike DeWine, who I unfortunately helped get elected years ago, when he was losing by 16 points prior to my doing a Rally for him was, as usual, disloyal to the Republican Party," Mr. Trump wrote. "He strongly suggested that Vivek should, 'take down the Ad.' He probably wants a Dumocrat to win, and certainly doesn't want someone who will do a much better job than he is capable of doing. I suggested, on the other hand, that Vivek should keep it up..."

Mr. Trump added he only wishes the "mothers of my opponents would be so brave as to come forward and explain that their son or daughter is a liar, and much worse." 

"Who wouldn't use such an Ad?" Mr. Trump wrote. "I would, it's called, 'hitting pay dirt.'"

Mr. Trump continued to defend the ad during a rally in Iowa late Thursday. He said he advised Ramaswamy that "you gotta ride with it," later adding: "Leave it up, and look upstairs and say, 'Thank you God, very much.'"

Vance, too, defended the ad, saying Republicans who have criticized it should "stop whining." 

Ohio Republican Sen. John Husted, who is running for reelection, said he "would not have run that ad." 

Outgoing Rep. Nancy Mace of South Carolina called the ad the "most shameful, disgusting, offensive ad this election season."

Ohio Secretary of State Frank LaRose, a Republican, told a local ABC station he "probably wouldn't run an ad like that, but every candidate gets to make their own decision."

Acton's brother said earlier this week it's "not surprising that Vivek Ramaswamy has stooped to such a despicable low as to attempt to turn the sexual abuse Amy endured at twelve years old from our birth mother's husband into a political talking point." 

"Our birth mother stayed married to Amy's rapist until he died," Stearns said. "This desperate, disgusting attack reveals exactly who Vivek Ramaswamy is at his core – a pathetic excuse for a man who is willing to hurt anyone as long as it gets him what he wants."

data.title: Pastor Adam Hamilton could be Kansas's 1st Democratic senator since the Depression
data.description:
Who is Adam Hamilton? A guide to the megachurch pastor who may become Kansas's first Democratic senator since the Great Depression.

Polls show Hamilton could end a 90-year Republican winning streak in the Sunflower State — and help Democrats flip the Senate on Nov. 3.

Andrew Romano
Updated Thu, October 22, 2026 at 9:38 PM UTC
8 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

When it comes to picking senators, no state is nearly as consistent as Kansas. The last Democrat to win there, a former county attorney named George McGill, was elected in 1932. Kansas's other senator, a Republican incumbent, won reelection in 1936. McGill lost to a Republican in 1938. And Kansas has been sending Republicans to the U.S. Senate ever since. 

That's a 90-year winning streak. 

But the composition of Kansas's Senate delegation could change on Nov. 3 — and with it, Republican control of the chamber as a whole. To the surprise of pretty much the entire political world, first-term GOP incumbent Roger Marshall is currently locked in a too-close-to-call contest with megachurch-pastor-turned-rookie-candidate Adam Hamilton — a former Republican who considered running as an independent before deciding to seek the Sunflower State's Democratic nomination.

Advertisement

Hamilton, 61, is one of several heartland Democrats or Democratic-leaning independents who are giving Senate Republicans a run for their money in ruby-red states that President Trump won by double-digit margins in 2024 (including Texas, Iowa, Nebraska and even South Carolina). He describes himself as "a liberal conservative and a conservative liberal."

"I'm not somebody who favors the Socialist Party," Hamilton said Wednesday night during a debate against Marshall. "I'm somebody who stands in the middle. I'm going to try to work for all Kansans, Republicans, independents and Democrats."

Here's everything you need to know about one of the key figures of the 2026 midterms. 

Who is Adam Hamilton?

In some ways, Hamilton is similar to James Talarico, the Democratic Senate nominee in Texas, who is equally unapologetic about his Christian faith. But where Talarico has studied at seminary on the side — his main gig has been serving in the Texas House of Representatives — Hamilton is a bona fide church leader. 

Born in 1964 and raised in the Kansas City suburb of Prairie Village, Hamilton didn't go to church regularly as a child. His parents were teenage high school dropouts when they had him; they divorced by the time he was a teenager. Hamilton started drinking and taking drugs in seventh grade; two years later he got clean and started attending Pentecostal services on the recommendation of a door-to-door evangelist. Before long, Hamilton was heading up the church's youth group; he married a fellow attendee a week after high school graduation. Eventually, he earned a bachelor's degree in pastoral ministry from Oral Roberts University in Tulsa and a Master of Divinity from Southern Methodist University in Dallas. 

In 1990 — when Hamilton was just 25 — his United Methodist denomination tapped him to start a church for nonchurchgoers in suburban Kansas City. Worshippers initially met in the small chapel of a local funeral home. Today, Hamilton's United Methodist Church of the Resurrection is the largest United Methodist congregation in the U.S., with an average weekly attendance of about 25,000 people online, on television and across its nine area campuses. Its Christmas Eve offering, which is devoted to mission work, has topped $2 million.

Hamilton has also written more than 30 books that have together sold millions of copies; his video-based lessons are used in Sunday school classes nationwide. In 2013, he preached at the National Prayer Service after President Barack Obama's second inauguration. Three years later, Obama appointed Hamilton to his Advisory Council on Faith-Based and Neighborhood Partnerships.

Hamilton was registered as a Republican as recently as 2020; when he was first considering a 2026 Senate bid, he formed an exploratory committee as an independent. At the time he told his congregation — "a nearly equal mix of Republicans, Democrats and Independents," according to the Associated Press — that he could "bridge partisan divides in a highly polarized political climate" (as the AP put it). 

"Every week, it seemed there was another news story in the last year where I would find myself shaking my head and thinking, we have to do better," the self-described fifth-generation Kansan told the AP.

But Hamilton was persuaded to run as a Democrat so as not to split the anti-Marshall vote in the general election. He wound up massively outraising his Democratic primary opponents and winning the party's Aug. 4 primary by more than 20 percentage points. 

What does Hamilton stand for?

In college, Hamilton chose not to become a Pentecostal preacher because the denomination felt too black and white. In contrast, Methodism struck him as a thinking person's church, he told a local Kansas City paper in 2002. "It seemed to me there was some gray in the world," Hamilton explained. "It is OK if you have doubts. It's OK if you have questions. We don't have to check our brains at the door."

He now says he is an "independent-minded Democrat" who is "going to work across the aisle." 

At the Wednesday debate, Hamilton criticized Marshall for supporting the Trump administration's least-popular policies — tariffs, the war in Iran, immigration raids in farm country — while trying to distance himself from national Democrats. He called former President Joe Biden's immigration policy a "disaster," for instance, and promised not to "support Chuck Schumer for Senate majority leader if the Democrats [were] to control the Senate." When asked about transgender girls playing women's sports, Hamilton said he would not want his 12-year-old granddaughter competing against people assigned male at birth. "It's not a fair fight," he argued.

At times, Hamilton — who reminded the audience that he has "been a pastor for the last 38 years" and has "not been a senator" — struggled to provide specifics on issues such as farm subsidies, the Social Security wage cap and AI regulation, according to the New York Times. 

But Hamilton's general approach — his focus on "decency," affordability and "bringing people together" — has its roots in his ministry. Following the recent surge of federal immigration agents to Minneapolis, he cited on his podcast an Old Testament verse that commands Israelites to treat foreigners with love and fairness. In April, he said that he had voted against a state constitutional amendment that would have cleared the way for tougher abortion restrictions, arguing lawmakers should not be "the ethicists and the spiritual guides" for women (even as he lamented that his mother considered having an abortion when she was pregnant with him). And he has criticized Republican cuts to federal safety-net programs such as food stamps and Medicaid. 

"I just want to know, when did it become 'woke' to care for your neighbor?" Hamilton asked the AP, claiming that "Marshall would call [Jesus] 'woke'" if he were alive today.

How could Hamilton perform in the midterms? 

Hamilton's local prominence, fundraising prowess, "centrist" message and skill on the stump have made this year's Kansas Senate contest very competitive. ("No one has more practice at extemporaneous talking than a megachurch pastor," the Times noted.) Marshall leads by 1 percentage point in the most recent poll to be released — but it's the only survey conducted over the last month that shows the Republican candidate ahead. The rest (save one tie) give Hamilton a slight edge (between 1 and 5 percentage points).

Both candidates have faced controversy. Marshall has pushed back on reports that he sued hundreds of patients over unpaid medical bills during his decades-long career as an obstetrician-gynecologist, calling the allegations "blatant lies." And Hamilton has admitted he made a "mistake" by failing to bar a volunteer who had previously been accused of sexual abuse in 2005 from going on a retreat where he allegedly abused another boy.

"I was actually preaching that weekend at Church of the Resurrection, and I did not sign off on him going back. I should have checked to make sure that he wasn't going back," Hamilton said during Wednesday's debate. "That was a mistake on my part. But I will tell you, when he was investigated the next year, we forbade him from working with youth or children anymore. He left our church angry and upset. And again, we played a critical role several years later in getting him arrested and convicted."

Kansas hasn't sent a Democratic senator to Washington, D.C., since the Dust Bowl days — a conservative bent that's also reflected in its heavily Republican state legislature and the fact that it has voted Republican in every presidential election since 1940 except for Lyndon B. Johnson's 1964 landslide.

But the state has elected two Democratic governors in recent years — Kathleen Sebelius (2003-2009) and term-limited incumbent Laura Kelly (2019-2027) — and there is a tradition of ticket-splitting that goes back even further. (Since 1957, neither major political party has held the Kansas governor's mansion for longer than eight consecutive years.) 

Could Hamilton benefit from that sort of checks-and-balances heterodoxy on Nov. 3? It's possible. In Wednesday's debate, Marshall embraced the Trump agenda and explicitly told viewers that "if you want [it] to continue, you need to come out, because we delivered on those things." But even in Kansas, 53% of likely voters currently disapprove of how the president is handling his job. The fate of Hamilton's campaign, and perhaps his party's hopes of winning the Senate, will turn on whether he can convince those voters to cast their ballots for him on Election Day — even if they haven't voted for a Democrat in a long, long time.

data.title: Supreme Court sides with Republicans in New Hampshire student ID voting fight
data.description:
POLITICS
Supreme Court of the United States

Supreme Court sides with GOP in New Hampshire student ID voting fight

Maureen Groppe
USA TODAY
Oct. 22, 2026, 6:23 p.m. ET

WASHINGTON – The Supreme Court said New Hampshire can fully enforce a ban on voters using student IDs as a form of identification at the polls next month, a win for the Republican Party's effort to tighten voting procedures.

The court on Oct. 22 agreed to pause a lower court’s ruling that a student ID is among the forms of identification that may be considered by poll workers if the voter lacks an approved government-issued ID.

The state's U.S. Senate race is among the contests that will decide whether Republicans keep control of that chamber after the midterm elections. The Republican National Committee had backed the state's unsuccessful emergency appeal to the Supreme Court.

New Hampshire, controlled by Republicans, is among several states that have banned registered voters from using a student ID to verify their identity at the polls. A voting-rights group challenged the change as discrimination against younger voters and as an unconstitutional burden on their right to vote.

A federal judge in New Hampshire declined to block enforcement of the law as the case is litigated.

But the judge also said the new law had not changed the fact that a poll worker may accept or reject a student ID as a valid form of identification on a case-by-case basis through the state’s "safety-valve" provision.

New Hampshire Secretary of State David Scanlan asked the Supreme Court to intervene.

Scanlan, a Republican, said the judge's Oct. 2 order injected uncertainty into the state’s voting procedures less than three weeks before the election. He also said the judge wrongly interpreted the state's law.

Coalition for Open Democracy, the group challenging the law, said the judge correctly concluded that state officials failed to identify "any security or integrity concerns specific to student ID cards and why they are unique among other non-governmental forms of identification" that are allowed on a case-by-case basis.

The judge also found that the change had already kept one student from voting and could affect more because young voters may not have the government-issued IDs that are automatically accepted.

In the brief and unsigned opinion, the Supreme Court pointed to its previous rulings that federal courts should not alter rules on the eve of an election.

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only justice to publicly disagree with that decision. She said the federal judge had not changed the rules but only corrected the secretary of state's misinterpretation of them.

"I respectfully dissent because − even, and perhaps especially, when an election is looming − I would not disturb aclearly justifiable federal-court order issued to ensure that the public receives accurate information about a State'selectoral processes," she wrote.

data.title: DOJ investigating Corey Lewandowski's role in DHS contracting under Kristi Noem
data.description:
Corey Lewandowski speaks to the press in July 2024..(Photo by Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
See all topics
Email
Link Copied!

Justice Department prosecutors are investigating allegations of contract misconduct at the Department of Homeland Security, including the role of Corey Lewandowski who worked as de facto chief of staff to former Secretary Kristi Noem, according to multiple people familiar with the investigation.

The probe follows a criminal referral for Lewandowski from the DHS Inspector General’s office, which has been examining contracting practices at the agency during Noem’s and Lewandowski’s tenure, according to one of the people familiar.

The Justice Department declined to comment on the matter.

“Mr. Lewandowski has not been contacted by the Justice Department regarding any investigation, and he denies any wrongdoing when he was proudly serving his country in a voluntary capacity,” Lewandowski’s attorney Adam Trigg told CNN.

The Department of Homeland Security didn’t immediately return a request for comment on the matter.

The referral is an unusual move for the Trump administration, which has been hesitant to criminally investigate its own members.

Critics have instead largely accused the Justice Department of improperly targeting the president’s political enemies and accused DHS of protecting their own employees from scrutiny.

In recent months, as the allegations of possible corruption emerged, Washington, DC, US Attorney Jeanine Pirro told officials in her office that she wanted investigators to look into claims of kickbacks connected to contracting at DHS, according to a second source familiar with the investigation.

It’s still not clear which US Attorney’s office is leading the investigation.

Prosecutors have been awaiting results from the DHS inspector general probe, the person familiar with the probe said.

Related article
Corey Lewandowski, left, and Kristi Noem.

DHS internal watchdog launches investigation into handling of contracts under Noem, Lewandowski

3 min read

Lewandowski, a Republican operative, became a fixture at DHS early in President Donald Trump’s second term, serving as Noem’s chief adviser. But on paper, he was originally tapped to serve as a special government employee — a unique role meant to span a limited number of days.

Lewandowksi’s straddling of senior government functions at DHS and service as a special government employee was uncharted territory, according to multiple people who spoke with CNN.

Homeland Security officials ultimately viewed Lewandowski, a Trump ally, as Noem’s gatekeeper. He left the department when Trump fired Noem.

Noem’s handling of contracts within DHS was one of the main catalysts for her ouster by Trump earlier this year, notably when she claimed that Trump knew of a $220 million ad campaign prominently featuring the secretary.

During her tenure, Noem also tightened her grip on her department’s purse strings, ordering that every contract and grant over $100,000 had to cross her desk for approval — a move that Noem frequently defended as intended to cut down on waste but that multiple Homeland Security officials found unusual and unnecessary.

The inspector general, Joseph Cuffari, complained to Congress in early March that Homeland Security leadership had been obstructing some of his work.

Trump, when asked by a reporter on Thursday about the Lewandowski investigation, said he didn’t know much about it as he only just learned of it. He repeatedly said, however, that if people working for him are dishonest, he wants them prosecuted.

“They’re stealing from me, so I want my people to be honest,” Trump said. “And if they’re not honest, I’ll have my DOJ go and do whatever they have to do.”

This story has been updated with additional details.

data.title: Iran says 7 oil tankers attacked in the Strait of Hormuz as fears grow of a return to war
data.description:
Iran says 7 oil tankers attacked in the Strait of Hormuz as fears grow of a return to war

MELANIE LIDMAN
Updated Thu, October 22, 2026 at 8:52 AM UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

The top photos of the day by AP's photojournalists

1 of 2
An actor portraying U.S. President Donald Trump sits behind bars in a billboard installation resembling a prison cell in Tajrish Square in Tehran, Iran, Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026. (AP Photo/Vahid Salemi) (AP Photo/Vahid Salemi)

TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — Seven oil tankers caught fire or were damaged in the Strait of Hormuz overnight after being hit by Iran or striking naval mines, Tehran said Thursday, a markedly high number as tensions rise over concerns about a return to all-out war.

With days before a close election in Israel in which Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu could lose power, and before next month's U.S. midterm election in which war-linked high prices have sparked voter anger, there are concerns that U.S.-Israeli attacks on Iran could resume.

"Netanyahu wants to attack Iran, that's not even a question," Danny Citrinowicz, a researcher at Israel's Institute for National Security Studies and a former Iran specialist in Israel's military and intelligence services, told The Associated Press.

Advertisement

He accused Israel of rushing into another round with Iran without revamping its strategy. A clear Netanyahu victory in the Oct. 27 election means an attack is almost guaranteed, he said.

Main opposition candidates are likely to focus on domestic issues first, but Citrinowicz said he believed the region is on the way toward "another kinetic escalation."

Iran repeats threat to attack U.S. bases in the region

Iranian state television reported the claims about the latest attacks on ships, which the AP couldn't independently confirm. The report cited the Revolutionary Guard Corps navy, which again threatened to strike U.S. military bases in the region if the U.S. keeps helping to guide commercial ships through the strait.

The report didn't mention casualties. Iran still asserts control over the waterway, a central point of leverage in any talks with the U.S. over the war.

October has had the most reported attacks on commercial shipping since March in the war's opening weeks, according to a British military monitor, the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations. UKMTO didn't report the latest attacks, but it has noted new reluctance by some shippers to report incidents.

Oil producers have found ways to keep crude flowing, experts say, but at a mounting cost.

Tankers continue moving through Strait of Hormuz despite attacks

Oil tankers are still moving oil through the strait under U.S. military protection despite the recent upsurge in attacks, according to shipping data and analysis company Lloyd's List Intelligence.

Tanker operators willing to risk the voyage have been shuttling oil from Gulf producers through the strait at night with their location systems and mobile phones turned off using a U.S.-protected lane near the coast of Oman. Those tankers transfer oil to other tankers waiting in the Gulf of Oman for shipment to customers in Asia.

Those "active Gulf operators show little sign of retreating" despite 28 attacks on ships in October, the highest since the start of the war, Lloyd's said in an online webinar Thursday.

The so-called "dark shuttle" overseen by U.S. Central Command has helped keep oil shipments from the Gulf at roughly prewar levels, but at high costs in time, money and sailors' lives. Spot charter rates for tankers have soared into the hundreds of thousands of dollars a day, while the ship-to-ship transfers can take several days.

Iran says it's open to diplomacy but also self-defense

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi on Wednesday said that a wary Tehran remains open to diplomacy, but is ready to defend itself.

Iran has warned that it has learned important military lessons from the war that began with U.S. and Israeli attacks on Feb. 28. In recent days, Tehran has indicated that it could expand targets to include infrastructure such as undersea cables and data centers.

The United States, for its part, is sending more military assets to the region, including a third aircraft carrier and thousands of troops, to join the largest force of American warships and aircraft in the Middle East in decades.

Mediators, meanwhile, have been trying to bring Washington and Tehran back to formal talks.

Iran still promotes its latest proposal that would end the war and fully open the strait within a week if the U.S. meets several conditions. Those conditions, which include ending the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports, echo ones in the deal that fell apart within days of both sides signing it in June.

In late September, U.S. President Donald Trump rejected that seven-day proposal, but both sides have acknowledged that indirect discussions have continued.

The stakes are even higher if all-out war resumes

A return to full fighting would again endanger civilians throughout the region and complicate global deliveries of oil, natural gas and related products like fertilizer from the region and likely bring another spike in prices.

The head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, Mohsen Rezaei, this week acknowledged that the Islamic Republic will suffer under a prolonged U.S. blockade. But economic pain and strategic collapse are not the same thing, he added, according to Iran's state-run IRNA news agency.

Now the landscape of the conflict has widened with the recent surge in fighting between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and Saudi Arabia. The Saudi kingdom backs a coalition of forces with Yemen's internationally recognized government that is fighting the rebels.

The Houthis' repeated deadly attacks on airports and other facilities inside Saudi Arabia have pressured the close U.S. ally, which has sought military aid.

The escalation also has threatened a crucial shipping corridor, the Bab el-Mandeb at the southern end of the Red Sea.

data.title: U.N. calls El Niño a 'behemoth' as forecasts point to unprecedented strength
data.description:
WEATHER
El Nino (weather)

'Behemoth' El Niño to upend global weather, UN warns

Extreme weather events already being reported are expected to "multiply – and cascade – as El Niño intensifies," the World Meteorological Organization warned.

Dinah Voyles Pulver Doyle Rice
USA TODAY
Oct. 21, 2026Updated Oct. 22, 2026, 10:03 a.m. ET

The warnings about El Niño continue to roll in. The United Nations' weather agency weighed in on Oct. 21, calling the potent climate pattern a "behemoth" and a "wrecking ball."

"It will tear through Latin America, Eastern and Southern Africa, Asia and the Pacific with extreme heat, droughts and flood," the U.N.'s Tom Fletcher said, warning of profound humanitarian consequences.

El Niño, a natural warming of Pacific Ocean waters that affects weather and climate patterns worldwide, tends to cause higher global temperatures and disrupt rainfall patterns across large regions, meaning drought in some areas and heavy rains in others.

It triggers disruptive weather patterns that often impact agriculture, infrastructure and supply chains, potentially causing trillions of dollars in damages around the globe.

El Niño is forecast with "high confidence" to be at record-breaking strength and peak this winter, NOAA's Climate Prediction Center said.

"This will certainly be an historic El Niño," Michael Mann, a climate scientist and professor at the University of Pennsylvania, told USA TODAY. It will be the "biggest event on record," but because reliable records only go back less than a century, it's difficult to assess how unusual it is in a longer-term context, Mann said.

'Unprecedented in strength'

As ocean temperatures continue to warm in the eastern Pacific, the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) warned on Oct. 21 that the developing El Niño could be "unprecedented in strength."

“This is literally off the monitoring charts that we have used for the past four decades," said Celeste Saulo, secretary of the WMO. The event is forecast to peak later in 2026, "but its impacts will be felt long after that," Saulo said.

The WMO expects the El Niño event to become extremely strong, with temperatures in the central Pacific rising more than 6 degrees (3.8 Celsius) above normal between November and January, peaking around December.

Global financial impact: 'Super El Niño' will have an alarming financial impact, experts fear

Extreme weather events already being reported are expected to "multiply – and cascade – as El Niño intensifies," the WMO warned.

Forecasts for the event are "very high confidence now and the very strong El Niño will certainly last through the next several months," said Emily Becker, deputy director of the Cooperative Institute for Marine & Atmospheric Studies at the University of Miami's Rosenstiel School for Marine, Atmospheric & Earth Science.

El Niño is likely to strengthen further, but at this point, forecasters already have as much information as they'll ever have about the expected impacts, and the seasonal outlooks reflect that, Becker said. She added that it's "important to remember that the weather is always full of surprises, and even in a strong El Niño it’s critical to monitor short-term weather and sub seasonal forecasts."

El Niño adding to climate change effects

One of the important things to note about this El Niño event is that it's converging with the impacts of human-caused climate change, such as sea level rise, said Fraser Shilling, director of the UC Davis Road Ecology Center, at the Institute of Transportation Studies, in a recently published study for California.

El Niño warming "adds to human-caused warming in such a way that we see new records set every time we get a major El Nino event," said Mann. He was a lead author on a study released earlier this year that found El Niño "contributed substantially to the record 2024 global temperatures."

"The science is very unclear about whether we are seeing or expect to see an increase in the amplitude of El Nino events from human-caused warming," Mann said, with many models predicting the opposite will occur.

The extreme levels of warmth associated with major El Niño events are temporary, he said, but the events such as those discussed in the United Nations announcement give us a glimpse of "what our future will look like if we continue to warm the planet."

US impacts from El Niño

In the United States, a very strong El Niño tilts the odds toward stormier weather across the South, said Ken Graham, director of NOAA’s National Weather Service. Graham warned the nation earlier in October to prepare for its impacts. “While higher chances of rain and snow may bring relief to drought-afflicted areas, too much precipitation on dry soil can fuel destructive flash floods and mudslides," he said.

In California, Gov. Gavin Newsom recently declared a state of emergency to prepare for the impacts from the event.

Shoreline flooding already seen along the Southern California coast with this El Niño raises concerns for the coming months, according to the report Shilling released. California's Highway 37 and other coastal roadways are "extremely vulnerable to floods and failure during this winter’s coming El Niño," Shilling said. “It’s important to be informed of risk so you can make decisions.”

WMO report details global impacts

The WMO's outlook warned of the following potential impacts this winter:

  • The Americas: Increased rainfall in the southern parts of western South America and in portions of North America and the northern portion of the Caribbean, while drought risk increases in parts of Central America, the southern Caribbean and the Amazon.  
  • East Africa: Wetter-than-normal conditions likely during the October–December rainy season, increasing concerns about heavy rainfall and flooding.  
  • Southern Africa: Increased risks of drier conditions could affect crop production, water availability and livelihoods from the typical start of the rainy season in November.  
  • Southeast Asia: Warmer conditions and rainfall deficits increase the risk of heat exposure and place additional pressure on agriculture and water supplies, like the increase in wildfire and smoke-haze risks we are already seeing.

Contributing: Reuters

Doyle Rice and Dinah Voyles Pulver are national correspondents for USA TODAY, focusing on climate and weather. Reach them at drice@usatoday.com and dpulver@usatoday.com.

(This story was updated to clarify information from NOAA about this year's El Niño .)

data.title: Judge orders Trump to sit for deposition in BBC defamation lawsuit by Dec. 11
data.description:
Judge orders Trump to sit for a deposition in his defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11

DAVID FISCHER and JOCELYN NOVECK
Updated Thu, October 22, 2026 at 2:19 PM UTC
4 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

Trump

1 of 2
President Donald Trump speaks to reporters after arriving on Air Force One, Wednesday, Oct. 21, 2026, at Joint Base Andrews, Md. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson) (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)

MIAMI (AP) — A federal judge on Thursday ordered President Donald Trump to sit for a deposition in his $10 billion defamation lawsuit against the BBC by Dec. 11.

The order from U.S. Magistrate Judge Enjoliqué Lett came as the BBC's lawyers complained that Trump had delayed his appearance. Attorney Charles Tobin said that with two months left in the discovery period, "we still haven't been able to depose the plaintiff."

He noted there was an agreed-upon date of Oct. 16, but that the Republican president canceled it for a "matter of national importance." Tobin said Trump was in fact campaigning in Georgia that day.

Advertisement

"He was participating in party politics and prioritized that over sitting for the deposition," Tobin said.

Lett said Trump must sit for a deposition by Dec. 11, or face sanctions up to dismissal of his lawsuit -– unless the discovery period was extended past Dec. 18.

The BBC asked the judge last week to compel Trump to appear after they said he canceled an agreed-upon date of Oct. 16, citing "matters of national importance." The British broadcaster says Trump is trying to delay his appearance until January 2027. The judge has threatened sanctions if Trump fails to comply with the court's schedule.

Trump, who has often avoided depositions, filed his lawsuit against the BBC last December, seeking $10 billion in damages. He accused the publicly funded broadcaster of defamation as well as deceptive and unfair trade practices related to a documentary, "Trump: A Second Chance."

The BBC acknowledged that filmmakers spliced together quotes from different sections of the speech Trump delivered to his supporters on Jan. 6, 2021, before the storming of the U.S. Capitol, to make it seem he was directly urging violence. The broadcaster apologized over the editing, and the head of the BBC and its top news executive both resigned. The BBC has denied Trump's claims that it defamed him.

Trump's lawyers say Jack Smith 'lacks personal knowledge' of issues in the case

To bolster its defense, the broadcaster subpoenaed former special counsel Jack Smith earlier this month. Trump's lawyers argued, in a joint filing asking for a hearing on the matter, that there was no good reason for Smith, who is not a party to the case, to appear.

"Smith lacks any personal knowledge regarding the issues in this matter," they argued in the filing. "He was not present when President Trump's January 6, 2021, speech … was made, nor did he participate in its preparation. Smith does not have any personal knowledge regarding President Trump's state of mind at the time the Speech was given."

Trump's side also argued that "Smith's testimony would be duplicative," because he published a lengthy report on the events of Jan. 6 and also testified for many hours. "The entirety of his testimony is publicly available," it argued.

The BBC countered, in the same filing, that there were few more knowledgeable sources about the events of Jan. 6 than Smith, who studied and investigated them for years.

"It is difficult to imagine a more authoritative source on these issues than Mr. Smith, who spent years gathering evidence on those topics with the force of the Justice Department and the power of the grand jury behind him," the BBC's lawyers argued.

"No one forced Plaintiff to file this lawsuit and to dispute that his speech on January 6 incited the violence that followed at the Capitol. But as long as he chooses to maintain the case, he cannot commit the fundamental injustice of preventing the BBC from obtaining the evidence it needs to robustly defend itself on every element of his claim…"

When will Trump sit for a deposition?

In a filing Oct. 13, the BBC's lawyers said they first requested dates for a deposition in July, and followed up repeatedly, with both sides eventually agreeing on Oct. 16.

After weeks of silence, they wrote, "Plaintiff's counsel responded on September 28, 2026, indicating that 'the President is no longer available for his deposition on October 16 due to other matters of national importance' and that counsel would 'endeavor to provide you with a replacement date by the end of this week.' He did not."

They said they were then told that Trump "has no availability whatsoever for a deposition" before discovery is set to close on Dec. 18, and that Trump would instead make himself available the second or third week of January.

Tobin wrote in the filing, "Those delays have flouted the cooperative spirit of discovery and precluded the BBC from obtaining the evidence necessary to robustly litigate its defense."

___

Noveck reported from New York.
